Grow fresh herbs and veggies at home, whatever the season. Our experts reveal which indoor gardens make it easiest – and which are worth buying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you love home cooking, then what could be more appealing than picking fresh herbs and lettuce leaves – or even flavorful cherry tomatoes or chilis – right from your kitchen countertop? The best indoor garden systems let you grow your own organic produce year-round, even when it’s freezing outside. And unlike a backyard veggie garden, they take up hardly any space: just a small corner near a free power outlet.

Offering features like built-in grow lights, automated watering, and often hydroponic setups, indoor growing systems make it easy to produce fast and surprisingly substantial harvests. Prices, features, and growing capabilities vary considerably, but most systems are straightforward to use and designed with beginners in mind. Some models have a small footprint, while others offer more capacity for bigger harvests.

With so many systems to choose from, finding the right one for your needs can be confusing. The Gardening Know How team has tested some of the leading models and shares firsthand experiences with setup, growing performance, maintenance, and harvesting in this guide. We will help you compare the models, identify the features that matter most, and choose the best system for your space, budget, and growing ambitions.

Here we round up three of the best indoor garden systems. Scroll down to read more detailed reviews from testing each product hands-on. You can also use the links to jump to the indoor garden that interests you the most.

If you're new to indoor growing, the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is an easy way to get started, ideal for fresh herbs, salad greens, and even dwarf tomatoes. With automatic lighting and self-watering capability, it uses pre-seeded pods, making it easy to get started and delivering great results. Just bear in mind that the replacement seed pods add to the ongoing cost.

The Auk Mini combines a compact footprint with a stylish Scandinavian-inspired design, making it ideal for smaller kitchens (especially if you're fond of the IKEA aesthetic). It's exceptionally easy to use, and you can grow your own choice of seeds without buying special pods. With room for just four plants, though, it's better for fresh herbs as opposed to more substantial harvests.

If you love the idea of enhancing your growing with the latest tech, then the LetPot LPH-Max is the indoor garden for you. This impressive hydroponic system fits a variety of herbs, greens, and vegetables. Its advanced smart features offer plenty of control, but setup can be fiddly for some users, and some automated functions require extra equipment.

Drawing on our extensive gardening experience, we evaluated each system for ease of setup and use, build quality, efficiency, crop performance, and overall value for money. Each reviewer tested their indoor garden for at least eight weeks in their own kitchen, assessing everything from initial setup to ongoing maintenance and harvesting. As the systems were tested by different experts in their own homes, growing conditions varied slightly, but all reviewers followed the same assessment criteria.

From stylish, compact designs to more advanced hydroponic systems, here's how they performed in our kitchens – and who we'd recommend them for.

After four months of testing the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9, I can honestly say it's so low-maintenance it feels illegal. Setup took about 10 minutes, including time to read the instructions. Growing tomatoes, lettuce, herbs, and flowers is as easy as loading a coffee pod into a capsule machine: just pop the pre-seeded pods into the reusable grow cups and click them into place. It's completely mess-free, and the built-in grow light means you don't need a sunny windowsill.

Watering is just as easy. I refill the reservoir about once a week, and the system handles the rest. A handy water-level indicator takes away the guesswork. I even went out of town for two weeks, and my plants kept growing without any care.

I grew basil, lettuce, dwarf tomatoes, and marjoram. The lettuce grew quickly and made delicious summer salads, and the basil brought wonderful flavor to my Italian dishes. I was most impressed, though, by the cherry tomatoes. I transplanted a few spare seedlings into standard pots under grow lights, but the Smart Garden tomatoes grew much larger and produced fruit about two months earlier.

The only disappointment was the marjoram. It sprouted well but barely grew, possibly because the larger basil and tomato plants blocked its light.

Overall, the Smart Garden 9 has been a really fun, easy, and delicious project. Its sleek design looks great in my kitchen, and I'd highly recommend it to beginners or experienced gardeners looking for a hassle-free way to grow fresh produce year-round.

Reviewed by Kathleen Walters. Read the full review for more details.

The Auk Mini is easily one of the most stylish indoor growing systems I've come across. With its sleek Scandinavian design featuring wooden supports and a choice of black or white finishes, it's a world away from the more clinical-looking hydroponic systems on the market. You can also choose from three base finishes – cork, oak, or walnut – so it's easy to find one that looks at home in your kitchen.

Setting it up couldn't have been simpler. I just pushed the wooden supports into either side of the base, threaded through the power cable, and attached the adjustable grow light on top. Then it was a case of filling each of the four mini planters with the supplied coco coir and planting the seeds. Mine came with basil and parsley, so I was ready to start growing straight away. Adding the coir was a little messy, and there aren't any convenient pre-seeded pods like you get with some other systems. However, the big advantage is that you can use whatever seeds you like (within reason), rather than being tied to a brand's refills.

The water reservoir has an indicator that tells you when it's full or needs refilling, and you also get two little bottles of nutrients labeled Grow and Flavor – which felt delightfully Alice in Wonderland! You just pump these into the reservoir as directed. The grow light has different settings and a timer, and I particularly liked being able to position it low over the seedlings, then raise it as the herbs grew taller.

Within six to seven weeks, I was harvesting fresh herbs, which was very pleasing. I also loved how neat and self-contained the whole system was once it was set up. It's attractive enough to leave out on display rather than hide away in a utility room, and it has taken pride of place on my kitchen countertop.

The main limitation is its size. With room for just four plants, it's really designed for growing a few fresh herbs rather than producing substantial harvests. But if you want something compact, easy to use, and great-looking, then the Auk Mini is a lovely choice. There's now a newer Mini 2, but the original Mini is still available while stocks last.

The LetPot LPH-Max makes it easy to grow plenty of edible plants indoors year-round. With 21 small pods and an alternative tray for two larger plants, you can grow practically a whole garden right in your kitchen. It's mess-free, too – no dirt required. Just fill the tank with water, add plant food, and sow your seeds in the sponge-like pods.

The system was pretty easy to set up, though it took me about an hour to read the directions and work out how everything fit together. I was genuinely shocked by how well my basil grew in just water and plant food. Hydroponics is kind of amazing!

However, I did run into a few frustrations. I wanted to try the automatic watering and feeding, but it requires an extra 7-liter reservoir to refill the tank. With a rambunctious cat, limited space, and newly refinished hardwood floors, that wasn't practical, so I used manual mode instead. The top tray didn't fit properly, and I was also disappointed that seeds weren't included.

Ultimately, I think the LetPot LPH-Max is a good choice for those with hydroponics experience or who enjoy integrating technology into gardening. The app provides helpful growing information and remote controls, though a few features didn't work as expected. For beginners or anyone short on space, I'd recommend starting with a simpler system.

Reviewed by Laura Walters. Read the full review for more details.

The AeroGarden Harvest is a compact, beginner-friendly hydroponic system that grows up to six herbs, vegetables, or flowers, with a 20W LED grow light, automatic lighting, and handy reminders for adding water and nutrients.

The Ahopegarden Hydroponic Growing System has a double-layer design that offers a space-efficient alternative to other countertop gardens, with space for 44 pods.

The iDOO Hydroponic Growing System packs plenty of features into an affordable countertop garden, including Wi-Fi app control, adjustable LED grow lights, automatic timers, and a built-in fan and water pump, with space to grow up to 12 plants.

Indoor garden systems can make it easy to grow fresh herbs, salad greens, and even vegetables, but there's quite a difference between compact countertop systems and larger, fully automated hydroponic systems. Before buying, think about what you want to grow, how much space you have, and how much time you're willing to spend looking after your plants. These are the main things to consider.

Start by deciding where to position your indoor garden. Countertop systems are ideal for kitchens, but check the dimensions carefully – including the grow light's maximum height. These are often height-adjustable, but not always. You'll need enough clearance for plants to grow, as well as easy access to refill the water reservoir and harvest your crops.

Plant capacity is another important consideration. Smaller systems, such as the four-pot Auk Mini, are ideal for keeping a few fresh herbs on hand, while larger models can grow a wider variety of crops. However, just because an indoor garden has 20 growing positions doesn't mean you can actually grow 20 mature tomato plants. Larger crops like tomatoes need more room for their roots and foliage, so you may need to leave some planting spaces empty. But you can plant several herbs and lettuces as cut-and-come-again crops.

Indoor garden systems are mainly used for herbs and leafy greens, including basil, parsley, lettuce, and arugula. These grow relatively quickly, don't need much space, and can provide repeat harvests.

However, if you're hoping to grow tomatoes, peppers, or strawberries, you'll need to be more selective. Fruiting crops generally need more lighting, more growing space, and a longer growing period. Look for a system with an adjustable grow light and enough height to accommodate mature plants. Compact or dwarf varieties are usually the best choice.

Many indoor garden systems use hydroponics, meaning plants grow without traditional soil. Instead, their roots receive water with nutrients added using liquid feed, and they are often supported by sponges or another growing medium. These systems can be very efficient, but you'll need to keep the water reservoir topped up and add nutrients regularly.

Other systems use specially formulated growing media, such as Click & Grow's pre-seeded Smart Soil pods or the coco coir supplied with the Auk Mini. These can be particularly straightforward for beginners.

It's also worth checking whether you're restricted to the manufacturer's own seed pods. Some systems require you to buy compatible refills, while others allow you to use your own seeds, giving you more freedom to experiment with different varieties and potentially saving money over time.

One of the biggest advantages of an indoor garden system is that you don't need a sunny windowsill. Built-in LED grow lights provide all the light the plants need, and most systems include a timer to switch them on and off automatically.

Look for adjustable light height, particularly if you want to grow anything taller than herbs or lettuce. Some systems also offer different lighting modes for leafy growth and flowering or fruiting crops.

More advanced models include touchscreen controls, smartphone apps, automatic nutrient dosing, and water-level alerts. These features can be convenient, but they aren't essential for successful growing. A simpler system with reliable lighting and watering is often a better choice if you're new to indoor gardening.

Although indoor garden systems are low-maintenance, they aren't completely hands-off. You will still need to refill the water reservoir, add liquid fertilizer where required, prune plants, and harvest regularly. Hydroponic systems may also need periodic cleaning to prevent algae buildup and keep pumps and water lines working properly.

Consider how easy the reservoir is to access and clean, whether the system has a water-level indicator, and how often you'll need to refill it. If you travel frequently, a larger reservoir or automatic watering feature could be particularly useful.

Indoor garden systems range range from fairly affordable countertop models to high-tech setups costing several hundred dollars or more. However, the initial purchase price isn't the only expense to consider.

LED grow lights use electricity, although they're generally more energy-efficient than older lighting technologies. You can check the wattage and daily operating time to estimate running costs.

You'll also need to factor in the cost of replacement seed pods, the growing media, nutrients, and potentially other accessories. Proprietary pods can make planting wonderfully convenient, but the costs can add up if you're growing continuously.

Finally, think about what you actually want from your indoor garden. If your main goal is to save money on groceries, a small system growing a handful of herbs may take a long time to pay for itself. But if you enjoy gardening, want fresh ingredients year-round, or simply love watching things grow, the convenience and enjoyment can make it a worthwhile investment.

Yes. Indoor garden systems can be a worthwhile investment if you enjoy growing your own food and want a to be harvesting fresh herbs and leaves throughout the year. They're particularly useful if you don't have a garden or want to keep growing through winter. However, they're unlikely to save you a fortune on groceries, especially once you factor in electricity, nutrients, and replacement growing supplies. The real value lies in the convenience, enjoyment, and satisfaction of harvesting your own produce whenever you need it.

Indoor garden systems are ideal for growing herbs such as basil, parsley, cilantro, mint, and chives, along with leafy greens like lettuce, arugula, spinach, and kale. Some systems can also be used to grow smaller vegetables, including dwarf tomatoes, peppers, and even strawberries. The key is choosing plants that suit the available growing space and lighting. Fast-growing, compact crops tend to give the best results.

Most small indoor garden systems are inexpensive to run, thanks to energy-efficient LED grow lights. For example, a 20-watt light running for 16 hours a day uses approximately 9.6 kWh of electricity per month. At an electricity rate of $0.17 per kWh, that works out to around $1.63 a month. Larger systems with more powerful lighting, pumps, and automated features will use more electricity.

Yes, but you'll need the right system and varieties. Compact or dwarf tomatoes are particularly well suited to indoor growing, provided they receive enough light and have room to develop. Strawberries can also grow successfully indoors, although they need sufficient light, nutrients, and pollination to produce fruit. Look for a system with adjustable lighting and enough space for mature plants, and avoid overcrowding.

Yes. Because hydroponic plants grow without traditional soil, they rely on nutrients dissolved in the water to provide the minerals they need. Most systems come with a starter supply of specially formulated liquid nutrients. Avoid using ordinary garden fertilizer unless the manufacturer specifically recommends it, as it may not contain the right balance of nutrients or dissolve properly. Some systems automate nutrient dosing, while others require you to add it manually.

Absolutely. In fact, many indoor garden systems are designed specifically for people with little or no gardening experience. Models with pre-seeded pods, automatic grow lights, and self-watering reservoirs take much of the guesswork out of growing plants. The Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is a particularly beginner-friendly option, while systems such as the Auk Mini offer more flexibility to experiment with your own seeds. Start with easy crops like basil or lettuce, follow the instructions, and you'll soon be enjoying your first homegrown harvest.

Melanie is an experienced gardener and has worked in homes and gardens media for over 20 years. She previously served as Editor on Period Living magazine, and worked for Homes & Gardens, Gardening Etc, Real Homes, and Homebuilding & Renovating. Melanie has spent the last few years transforming her own garden, which is constantly evolving as a work in progress. She is also a passionate organic home grower, having experimented with almost every type of vegetable at some point. In her home, Melanie tends to an extensive houseplant collection and is particularly fond of orchids.

#7802. What Your Cat Can Teach You About Aging Well

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

How to recognize the subtle difference between normal aging and cognitive decline, and help your senior cat stay engaged, comfortable, and independent

Watch a healthy older cat move through her day.

She may take a little longer to rise from her favorite chair. She may think twice before jumping onto a countertop she once reached without hesitation. She sleeps more, chooses her routines carefully, and has become remarkably skilled at persuading the people around her to bring things closer.

But she is still interested in breakfast. She still appears when a favorite person enters the room. She watches birds through the window, investigates a new cardboard box, and may still insist that 4:57 a.m. is a perfectly reasonable time to discuss breakfast.

The difference matters, and I learned that the hard way with my own cat.

Houdini was an eighteen-year-old black long-haired male who had never given me reason to worry. Then he started calling out at night, insistent enough that I could not ignore it. It would have been easy to write off as just aging. Old cats do that.

I ran a full workup instead. It showed kidney values just slightly above normal and nothing else. Apart from the calling, he still seemed to be enjoying his life. Between the pattern of the vocalizing and a workup that ruled out anything else driving it, the diagnosis was feline cognitive dysfunction.

I lost Houdini to kidney failure about six months later.

His story is a small, real version of the point this whole article is making. The calling was not eccentricity, and it was not only age. It was cognitive change, arriving quietly, in a cat who by almost every other measure still seemed like himself.

Scientists increasingly distinguish between two ideas: lifespan, how long we live, and healthspan, the years we remain healthy, active, independent, and engaged with life.

It is a concept that applies beautifully to cats.

For a cat, aging well means more than reaching 15, 17, or even 20. It means continuing to move comfortably, use the litter box, groom, sleep peacefully, interact with family, explore familiar surroundings, and remain interested in the world.

And sometimes, the first sign that something is changing is not found in a laboratory.

Cats are remarkably good at making gradual change difficult to notice.

A dog that suddenly struggles to climb the stairs tends to make the problem obvious. A cat simply stops going upstairs. The favorite sleeping place moves from the top of the bookcase to the sofa. The cat who once greeted you at the door is always asleep when you come home.

The litter-box accident is blamed on stubbornness. The midnight crying is dismissed as eccentricity. The cat who no longer jumps onto the bed is just getting old.

Some slowing is expected with age. But new or progressive changes should not automatically be dismissed as a normal part of aging.

Jump less often or choose lower resting places.

Need easier access to food, water, litter boxes, or favorite furniture.

Changes to discuss with your veterinarian

Stare at walls or hesitate at familiar doorways.

Sleep much of the day but become restless after dark.

Become unusually withdrawn, clingy, anxious, or irritable.

Begin eliminating outside the litter box.

Show a marked decline in activity or interest.

Changes in memory, awareness, sleep, and behavior can occur with feline cognitive dysfunction, the feline counterpart of age-related dementia, but they may also be caused by pain or illness.[1]

Arthritis can make a cat stop jumping. Kidney disease, diabetes, or thyroid disease can change drinking, urination, activity, and sleep. High blood pressure can affect vision and behavior. Pain, hearing loss, and declining eyesight can all make an older cat behave differently.[2]

That is why "sheâs just getting old" can be one of the most misleading explanations in senior-cat care. Old age itself is not a disease. Sometimes a subtle behavioral change is the first clue that something treatable is happening.

How she asks for food and whether she greets you at the door.

Which chair she prefers and how often she plays.

Whether she has always talked at night, or only started recently.

Those ordinary observations are valuable because many age-related changes happen gradually. Once a month, stop and consciously look at your cat as though you had not seen her for several weeks.

Do her back or hindquarters look thinner?

Has nighttime activity or vocalization changed?

Does she still interact with people and other pets in the same way?

Does she ever seem confused in familiar places?

Is she still interested in food, play, windows, smells, and everyday family activity?

Look for change from your catâs own normal. A 17-year-old cat who has always slept most of the day is very different from a 12-year-old whose sleep pattern suddenly changes.

Owners cannot observe their cats 24 hours a day. A few simple tools can help fill in the gaps.

Some owners use a cat-friendly wearable activity monitor to track movement and rest over time. The value is never one isolated number. It is the pattern, and whether that pattern is shifting from the catâs own normal.

The simplest tool is your phone. Every few months, record your cat walking, jumping, climbing stairs, playing, or interacting with you. A video from six months ago often reveals gradual change that memory alone smooths over. Senior-cat care guidelines specifically encourage tracking mobility and behavior at home, because subtle changes are otherwise easy to miss.[2]

One of the most useful discoveries about feline aging concerns something owners can actually see and feel: muscle.

Researchers who repeatedly examined 209 pet cats, some for as long as seven years, found that muscle condition often began declining between about 7 and 10 years of age and deteriorated more rapidly as cats became older.[3]

Body weight did not always fall at the same time.

That means a cat can appear to maintain roughly the same number on the scale while quietly losing muscle. Muscle that helps an older cat stand, balance, jump, climb into the litter box, groom, and remain independent.

Look along the spine, shoulders, hips, and hind legs.

Does she pull herself onto furniture with her front legs instead of springing upward?

Has she stopped visiting favorite places because they are harder to reach?

These changes deserve attention even when body weight seems stable.

Aging well is not simply about surviving another birthday. It is about preserving the ability to do things.

Cats teach another useful lesson about aging: Independence sometimes depends on accepting help.

A cat who no longer jumps onto the bed may still want to sleep beside you. A small step or ramp can restore that choice.

A cat with painful joints may stop using a litter box not because she has forgotten her training, but because climbing over the side hurts.

A cat who becomes confused at night may do better when furniture stays in familiar places, and the path between sleeping areas, water, food, and litter boxes is simple and predictable.

Consistent placement of important resources.

Easy access to windows, scents, toys, and other forms of stimulation.

Regular social contact, on the catâs terms.

The goal is not to make an old cat behave like a young cat. It is to help an old cat do the things that make her life her own.

The science behind feline aging has become especially interesting in the past few years. A 2026 study comparing thousands of observations across cats, humans, and other mammals found that cat and human brains age in strikingly similar ways, estimating that a 15-year-old cat is at roughly the same stage of brain aging as an 80-year-old person.[5] That is not a simple cat-years-to-human-years formula, but it does suggest cats experience brain aging in ways surprisingly relevant to us.

Scientists have also found deposits of amyloid-beta, the protein associated with Alzheimerâs disease in people, in the brains of cats that had shown signs of cognitive dysfunction.[6] Cats are not tiny humans, but the overlap is strong enough that naturally aging cats may help researchers understand how brains age in both species.

None of this points to a single cause or a single fix. Muscle, movement, sleep, pain, metabolism, kidney function, and brain health all seem to influence each other in aging cats,[7] which is why healthy aging rarely comes from one supplement or treatment. It is a whole-animal process.

A major 2024 study examining nearly 8,000 cat deaths in the United Kingdom estimated average life expectancy at birth at about 11.7 years, although females lived somewhat longer than males and mixed-breed cats lived longer than purebred cats as groups.[8]

But averages do not predict the future of one individual cat.

One encouraging finding was that a cat who had already reached 15 still had, on average, about 2.7 additional years of expected life in that population.[8]

A 15th birthday does not necessarily mean the end is near.

How can we make the years ahead good ones?

There is something wonderfully symmetrical about all of this.

We are beginning to study cats because they may help us understand how brains and bodies age, and at the same time, they may already be teaching us the larger lesson.

Aging well may not mean remaining unchanged. It may mean adapting while preserving what matters:

And the desire to remain engaged with the world.

There may even be a benefit flowing in the other direction.

A 2025 study found that cat and dog owners showed a slower decline in some measures of memory and thinking than people who did not own pets. Among cat owners, the association included verbal ability and delayed memory.[9]

The study cannot prove that cats caused the difference, but it offers a delightful possibility:

While we study our cats to understand healthy aging, sharing our lives with them may also be connected with aspects of healthier aging in us.

That is part of why my colleagues and I at Veterinary Health Research Centers developed CATMA, Cats Advancing Toward Mindful Aging, to help owners and veterinarians recognize meaningful change earlier.

The next time you see your older cat asleep in a patch of sunlight, consider what she may be telling you.

She knows whether she can reach her favorite chair.

Whether her legs carry her where she wants to go.

Whether there are still interesting things to investigate.

Perhaps that is as good a definition of aging well as any of us has found.

1. Dhaliwal R, Boynton E, Carrera-Justiz S, et al. 2023 AAHA Senior Care Guidelines for Dogs and Cats. J Am Anim Hosp Assoc. 2023;59(1):1-21. doi:10.5326/JAAHA-MS-7343. https://doi.org/10.5326/JAAHA-MS-7343

2. Ray M, Carney HC, Boynton B, et al. 2021 AAFP Feline Senior Care Guidelines. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2021;23(7):613â638. https://doi.org/10.1177/1098612X211021538

3. Pye CR, Dowgray NJ, Eyre K, et al. Longitudinal changes in bodyweight, body condition, and muscle condition in ageing pet cats. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025;12:1654002. https://doi.org/10.3389/fvets.2025.1654002

4. Hoummady S, Rameau O, Besegher A, et al. A day in the life of an aged catâEnvironment of old domestic cats and welfare implications. Journal of Veterinary Behavior. 2026;83:20â25. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jveb.2025.11.008

5. Januel C, Morrow E, Gibson R, et al. Cat brains age like humans: translating time shows pet cats live to be natural models for human aging. Biology Open. 2026;15(6). https://doi.org/10.1242/bio.062604

6. McGeachan RI, Ewbank L, Watt M, et al. Amyloid-Beta Pathology Increases Synaptic Engulfment by Glia in Feline Cognitive Dysfunction Syndrome. European Journal of Neuroscience. 2025;62(3). https://doi.org/10.1111/ejn.70180

7. Memoli H, Albertini M, Grader I, et al. Variations in body condition score, inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers predict cognitive changes in clinically healthy senior cats. Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience. 2025;17:1703764. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnagi.2025.1703764

8. Teng KT, Brodbelt DC, Church DB, OâNeill DG. Life tables of annual life expectancy and risk factors for mortality in cats in the UK. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2024;26(5). https://doi.org/10.1177/1098612X241234556

9. Rostekova A, Lampraki C, Maurer J, et al. Longitudinal relationships between pet ownership and cognitive functioning in later adulthood across pet types and individualsâ ages. Sci Rep. 2025;15:19066. doi:10.1038/s41598-025-03727-9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-03727-9

#7800. I Upgraded My $1.50 Microgreens Planter to a $69 Hydroponic Setup – But Was It Really Worth It?

I wanted a tidier, easier way to grow fresh greens indoors. Here's what I discovered when testing the Vego Garden EZ Microgreens Planter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I first started growing microgreens as something to do during the winter months when my restless green thumb began to feel neglected. What I didn’t expect was just how much I’d enjoy the process – or how rewarding it would be to have a steady supply of fresh, delicious greens right at my fingertips.

My microgreens fascination began with a little Dollar Tree mini greenhouse I picked up last spring, and honestly, it did the job. It was one of those inexpensive gardening finds that proved you don’t need a fancy setup to get started. As much as I enjoyed my budget setup, though, that dollar-store greenhouse grew brittle and flimsy the more I used it.

I started thinking there had to be a better way to grow microgreens by my kitchen window that would make the process easier. I'd seen plenty of clever options among the best indoor garden systems, but I wanted something specifically designed for microgreens. So, I traded my DIY mini greenhouse for the Vego Garden EZ Microgreens Planter – which you can buy directly from Vego or from Amazon at a discounted price for Black Friday – curious to see whether it was actually worth the upgrade...

This 7" x 5" mini greenhouse, complete with a waterproof seed-starting tray and clear humidity dome, was where it all began. Most people who bought one were probably planning to start flower or vegetable seeds, but I saw something else: a little tray with a humidity dome that looked perfect for growing a nice harvest of microgreens.

And it worked! Well, for a month or so, anyway.

There were a few drawbacks. For starters, the tray had no drainage holes, so I had to poke some into the thin plastic myself. That may have compromised its rigidity a little, and I also needed to place a second tray underneath to catch any excess water.

My first planting was a success, even using a packet of seeds I'd picked up at the dollar store. But after a few rounds, the plastic started to feel flimsy, and I quickly realized that dealing with soil indoors wasn't something I particularly enjoyed. It was messy, and, from what I'd been reading, you don't actually need soil at all to grow microgreens!

When my planter set arrived, I was eager to get started! One thing I immediately liked was that it came with not one, but two complete planter dome sets. That means you can grow twice as much or, if you don't need quite so many microgreens, share the second set with a gardening friend.

The kit also includes four 10" x 10" microgreens trays, two humidity dome covers, and 20 ready-to-use bamboo fiber growing mats. That's enough to grow up to four different varieties of microgreens side by side, which I thought was a lovely bonus. Just imagine having a selection of flavorful, brightly-colored greens ready to harvest!

If you're concerned about growing food in plastic containers, these planters are made from food-safe plastic, and the natural bamboo fiber growing mats mean you don't need to add soil. It's a simple, tidy way to grow fresh greens right on your kitchen counter.

Getting everything set up was surprisingly easy, too. The step-by-step instruction booklet was handy, but after just a quick glance, I realized I was probably overthinking things. This was going to be much easier than my first microgreens-growing experiment!

Everything I needed to get started was right in the box. First, I placed the water reservoir on the table, popped in the planting trays, and added the bamboo fiber mats, making sure the little wicking tabs were tucked underneath so they could reach the water below. Then came the fun part: sprinkling the seeds over the mats!

Once everything was in place, I filled the reservoir to the maximum fill line and gave the seeds a light misting to help settle them.

For this first growing round, I chose this pack of Mellow Blend Microgreens seeds from Botanical Interests. I thought this would be a great starter mix, containing broccoli, kohlrabi, red acre cabbage, and more. The greens are on the milder side, which suits my taste, but now that I have this planter, I definitely plan to experiment with some other varieties and blends.

And that's really it! No soil, no mess, just seeds, bamboo fiber mats, and water.

I popped the humidity dome on top, closed the vent to keep the moisture in, and placed the whole setup by my kitchen window alongside my other houseplants. If you don't have a sunny spot available, you can also use a grow light, like Vego's adjustable Grow Lights Stand, which is compatible with the microgreens planter.

It took about three days before I started seeing little sprouts appear, and in 8 days, I had leaves and a thick mass of roots. It's such a fun process to watch them grow. Microgreens really do seem to spring up before your eyes! The instructions recommend opening the dome vent as soon as you see new growth, so that's exactly what I did.

One other thing to keep an eye on is the water level. You want to make sure the little wicking tabs on the bamboo mats stay in contact with the water in the reservoir below. That way, your growing microgreens have a steady supply of moisture without you having to fuss over them too much.

For me, the answer is yes! If you enjoy growing microgreens, this is a nice little investment that makes the whole process easier, tidier, and more enjoyable. It's also a great gift idea for the avid gardener who seems to have everything else.

I especially like that I can use this planter set year-round. But now that summer is gone and the garden is put away for the winter, having fresh greens growing on my kitchen windowsill gives me the little gardening fix I need.

My one small gripe is the water-level viewing window on the reservoir. It's quite dark and tends to cast a shadow, making it difficult to see exactly how much water is left. I've found that shining my phone flashlight against it makes the level much easier to see, or I can simply lift the tray to check, but it's one little design detail I'd love to see improved in future versions.

After starting with a $1.50 mini greenhouse, I can honestly say the upgrade has been worthwhile. I have a much sturdier, neater setup, plenty of room to experiment with different microgreens, and a fresh supply of tasty greens right when I need them.

If you're a gardener who isn't quite ready to give up growing just because winter has arrived, I'd say this planter is well worth considering!

The ZestiGreens Self-Watering Microgreens Growing Kit makes it easy to grow fresh microgreens in just 7–10 days, with a stylish bamboo-framed tray, self-watering reservoir, reusable growing system, and everything you need to get started, including seeds and hemp growing mats.

For a simple, low-waste introduction to growing microgreens, the Back to the Roots Microgreens Grow Kit includes organic seeds, expanding coco coir discs, and compostable growing trays, with enough supplies for six harvests of fresh, flavorful greens in as little as seven days.

The Gardyn Complete Microgreens Growing Kit offers a convenient, soil-free way to grow fresh microgreens, with 20 pre-seeded pads in four varieties, bamboo wicks for self-watering, and 10 reusable grow plates that can be used on a sunny windowsill or with a Gardyn system.

#7799. When a Pet's Final Goodbye Becomes a Nightmare: The Philippines Crematorium Scandal

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

What began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell quickly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

By November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the company.

The questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

Sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

Different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

Another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

As tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

Biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

Exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

Not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

Pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

And this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

The scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

Families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) says the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

The Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

The death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

For some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

People entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.

Dull pruner blades and blunt shovels? Sharpen garden tools before you store them and you'll seriously appreciate the fresh edges in spring. From loppers to lawn mowers, here's exactly what to do.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After the last beds are cleared, gardening gear is often get left in a shed corner until April, but sharpen garden tools first and they'll be ready for action in spring. All it takes to fix pruners that crush stems and shovels that skip on clay is a file and a peaceful afternoon, and you'll be well rewarded for your time come the first warm weekend of 2027.

Sharp edges result in cleaner cuts that plants can heal more quickly, and a keen hoe or spade requires less effort to push through soil. A round of garden tool maintenance in late fall also helps you spot nicks, rust or loose bolts that showed up over the summer, and it's far easier to fix them in November than on the morning the roses need pruning. Garden tools you look after stick around a lot longer, too.

Here's how to sharpen blades of the most commonly used garden tools before you store them over winter.

To keep pruners in tip-top condition, it's best to use two types of sharpening tool. A double-sided diamond sharpener like this from Home Depot has a coarse side you can use to repair nicked edges as well as a fine face for the final touch-up. Use this to get and keep a good edge on blades. Then a smaller gadget like the Orange Ninja Garden Sharpener, available at Lowe's, or – even smaller – a pocket file like the Corona Garden Tool Sharpener from Amazon is handy mid-prune for a quick sharpen-up when cutting through tough stems.

Before you sharpen pruners, take a moment to examine the blades. Hold bypass pruners open and look at the cutting blade: one side has a slanted edge known as the bevel, while the other remains flat, sliding past the thicker hook. And it's that beveled side that needs sharpening. Place the tool securely on a workbench and draw a diamond file or small sharpening stone along the bevel at the factory's original angle, pushing toward the cutting edge.

Keep the flat side flat, only giving it one light pass to remove the burr that filing the bevel edge pushes up.

Hold anvil pruners open and you'll see that the cutting blade that closes against the flat anvil blade is beveled on both sides. File both beveled sides evenly so the edge between them meets the anvil at every point.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

To sharpen loppers, always start by cleaning them as sap and dried grit can hide damage and clog the file. Soapy water or turpentine removes sap, then a wire brush set like this from Walmart gets rid of the rest. Then hold the blade up to a bright window and look for chips, flat spots or daylight between the blade and the hook when it closes.

Sharpen loppers in exactly the same way as pruners, using the same double-sided diamond sharpener: file the beveled edge at its original angle, then remove the burr from the flat side. Small nicks come out fast with a file but deep chips and cracked blades are tougher to fix. So, if a blade is badly damaged, swapping in a replacement blade from the manufacturer usually works better than grinding away half the original edge.

To sharpen hedge shears, you need to work on the two long edges, one at a time. Because the blades are so long, you'll get a much better result if you use a bench vise like the Wilton 4-inch Bench Vise, available at Lowe's. Clamp one blade bevel-up in the vise and you'll have both hands free for your double-sided diamond file. Follow the original factory angle from the pivot all the way to the tip – then switch to the other blade.

When you're done, close the shears slowly and watch where the two edges meet. Blade tips that gape can mean a bent blade, which is more easily straighened in a vise after taking the shears apart. Snug the pivot bolt a little if the blades wobble, and ease it off if they bind.

Dull mower blades tear grass instead of cutting it, and the resulting damage means your lawn takes on a brownish-white cast where the torn tips die back. Regularly sharpening mower blades is one of the easiest ways to get lusher, greener grass without any extra effort, and when was the last time you sharpened yours?

Before you start this essential part of lawn mower maintenance, disconnect the lawn mower from its power source. That means pulling the spark plug wire on a gas mower, removing the battery on a cordless one, or making sure an electric mower is unplugged. Then carefully tip the mower on its side without letting oil spill. Put on cut-resistant work gloves like these safety gloves from Lowe's, and safety glasses, also available at Lowe's, because metal filings fly. Take the blade off your mower and secure in a vise with one of the cutting edges facing upward.

Your easiest option to sharpen lawn mower blades is a tool sharpener with a tungsten carbide blade like Garden Sharp, available from Ace Hardware. If you're confident about sharpening lawn mower blades, then a sharpener drill bit like the Sunbelt Sharpener, available from Lowe's, makes quick work of the task. There's no need to sharpen the entire length of the blade, just the outer 3-4 inches. Then turn the blade over to file the opposite cutting edge.

Lawn mower blade sharpening isn't done until the blade balances. Hang it on a blade balancer, often included with mower sharpening bits or you can buy a cheap Universal Metal Lawn Mower Blade Balancer from Amazon, or simply put a nail through the center hole. If one end of the blade drops, file just a little more from that side's cutting edge until it sits level. Lopsided blades shake the whole mower as they spin, and over time that can cause damage.

If the blade is bent, cracked, or won't balance correctly after filing, take it to a repair shop for sharpening and balancing, or buy a new one.

Spades and shovels typically end summer caked in soil and marked with rust, but it's a speedy and satisfying task to put that right before they go into the shed for the winter. Remove any dirt using a stiff brush, then scrub any rust spots with coarse steel wool like this from Amazon before filing, since grit can jam a file.

To sharpen a shovel or spade, use a diamond file or a dual-grit sharpening stone stone like this from Walmart, with a 100 grit side for aggressive metal removal and a finer 240 grit to finish. Position the spade with the inside face up and file away from your body along the existing bevel, following the tool's original profile. Some budget models arrive without a true edge and may need one filed in at around 30 degrees.

Not all digging tools need a sharp edge. Spades that slice through sod and roots benefit from one, but a scoop shovel for mulch works well with a blunter lip. Bear in mind, too, that an edge filed too thin wears down quickly.

A hoe doesn't need a razor edge, but enough sharpness to cut weeds below the surface instead of pushing them aside makes weeding much easier. To sharpen a garden hoe, clamp the head bevel-side up, then push a mill file across the blade in long strokes at the same angle the edge already has. The 8-inch Mill Bastard File from Home Depot works well here. Mill files cut only on the push stroke, so lift the file on the way back.

Which edge you're after depends on the hoe type. Standard draw hoes usually have a single bevel on one face, while stirrup and loop hoes cut on both the push and the pull, with edges on both sides of the strap. File until the edge feels smooth and even, then remove the burr from the back. Any sharpness beyond this level only leads to quicker wear.

Every tool should go into storage cleaner than it came out. Use a stiff brush to remove soil, then wash sap away with soapy water, and rub out any fresh rust using steel wool. Pruners, loppers and shears that touched diseased plants also need disinfecting, and 70% rubbing alcohol, available on Amazon, does that with less corrosion than bleach, which is hard on metal. If you use bleach, dilute it 1:10 with water and rinse and dry the blades well.

Once the metal is clean and dry, wipe on a light coat of oil to keep rust off, and put a drop on each pivot and spring. Walmart's 3-in-One Multi-Purpose Oil does both jobs from one small bottle. A thin coat of boiled linseed oil like Rustins Boiled Linseed Oil, available from Walmart, keeps wooden handles from drying and cracking, but read the label first as oil-soaked rags can catch fire on their own.

Store all tools off the ground in a dry spot – and perhaps now would be a great time to try some cheap and easy DIY projects to create more storage in your shed, too.

If you've always wondered how to sharpen gardening tools, now you know. Putting a fresh edge on garden tools is easy with the right sharpening tools and you'll be so glad you did come spring. When your pruners slice through a rose cane cleanly or your spade glides into dense clay without resistance on a bright April morning, that afternoon at the workbench will feel like time well spent.

#7796. Paws Off the Stuffing: A Guide to Safe Thanksgiving Foods for Dogs

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Letâs face it: despite its somewhat complicated and controversial history, these days,Thanksgiving is built around food, which makes it one of the trickiest holidays for dogs that want to join you around the table, since many common dishes contain ingredients that are toxic to them. Some foods are fine to share in small amounts, while others can cause anything from an upset stomach to life-threatening illness. Knowing which is which makes it easy to include a dog in the day without risking an emergency.

Turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions. The skin is fatty and usually coated in bastings and spices, and too much fat can lead to obesity and pancreatitis. Turkey bones can splinter and damage a dogâs mouth and digestive tract, so they should be avoided. Seasonings, including salt, can cause toxicity, so processed turkey should be skipped too. Plain meat is the safe choice, with no sauces or gravy.

Plain pumpkin is considered healthy, which is why so many dog foods contain it. Canned or fresh both work, provided the canned kind isnât pre-seasoned and nothing has been added. Pumpkin pie, with its spices and sugar, is a definite no.

Sweet potatoes are full of nutrients and vitamins, but they should be cooked and served in small amounts, without marshmallows, seasoning, or butter. Green beans offer vitamins, fiber, and manganese. They can be steamed, raw, canned, or cooked, as long as they are plain and not part of a casserole.

Corn is healthy without butter or salt, but only if it's been taken off the cob. Corn cobs are a relatively common source of intestinal blockage in dogs. Carrots, celery, and peas are fine cooked or raw and unseasoned, and carrots and celery should be cut into bite-sized pieces to prevent choking.

Plain cranberries are safe in moderation, though cranberry sauce and juice contain too much sugar. If they come from a dried fruit pack, only the cranberries should go to the dog. Apple slices are healthy and tasty, but the core and seeds should go in the trash. The seeds contain small amounts of cyanide that wonât harm a dog unless it eats too many, but itâs best to be cautious. The pie is for the people.

Cheese makes a tasty treat unless a dog is lactose intolerant, and low-fat versions suit dogs watching their weight. A small piece of plain bread is safe unless the dog has a grain allergy. It should have no raisins, seeds, or nuts, and since bread offers few nutritional benefits, it should only be an occasional snack.

Onions are highly toxic to dogs, along with everything in the onion family, including shallots, chives, and leeks, as they can cause anemia and liver damage. Garlic should also be avoided, and garlic powder is especially potent. It can also cause anemia, among other problems, so it shouldnât be anywhere near your pet.

Stuffing is also off limits. It usually contains onion, and it often carries a large amount of butter, which makes it too fatty for a dogâs diet. Mashed potatoes are fine if completely plain, but most are made with plenty of salt, butter, and other ingredients that arenât good for dogs, so itâs best to skip them. Gravy is a problem because of its high sodium, and it usually contains onions or garlic.

Chocolate is toxic because of two chemicals, theobromine and caffeine. It can lead to death if left untreated, and the signs can appear relatively quickly. Caffeinated drinks are risky for the same reason. Dogs are smaller and lighter than people, so it doesnât take much caffeine to cause trouble, and that rules out coffee, tea, and soft drinks.

Yeast-based bread dough is dangerous even though small amounts of baked bread are fine. The yeast expands in a dogâs stomach and can lead to bloat, which can progress to a life-threatening condition called gastric dilatation-volvulus. Alcohol of any kind causes poisoning in dogs, whether itâs a drink, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer.

A final but deadly ingredient to be aware of is the artificial sweetener, xylitol. Sometimes listed as birch sugar, even in small amounts, this seemingly minor ingredient causes severe hypoglycemia, and even if dogs survive this, irreversible liver damage can finish them off. Always keep an eye out for this one, commonly included in sugar-free mints, gums, candy, and peanut butter, to name a few.

A dog caught eating something toxic needs to go straight to a vet or the nearest emergency animal clinic. Bringing the packaging, along with a sample of whatever the dog ingested, helps the vet treat that particular substance. When itâs unclear whether something was toxic, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 can help. Both charge a fee, but they can guide the next steps and get a pet immediate help.

When it comes to ingested toxic ingredients, timing is everything. If you know your dog has eaten something potentially dangerous, or even if you just suspect it, donât wait for clinical signs to appear. By then, it may already be too late. Far better to pay for an overcautious detox than risk the life of a four-legged family member.

Thanksgiving can be enjoyable for the whole family, dogs included, as long as ingredients and leftovers arenât left out for a dog to gobble down. Be familiar with ingredients that are harmful to pets, particularly anything toxic. A little care with what gets shared keeps the day safe and lets everyone relax.

#7795. War Dogs of History: York and the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

The Korean War is often called Americaâs Forgotten War, with the dogs who served in it forgotten right along with it. Yet one platoon, and one dog in particular, quietly reshaped how the military would think about scout dogs for the rest of the twentieth century.

When North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, the United States military had almost nothing left of the war dog program that had served so effectively in World War II. After 1945, the Army had gutted its dog units, and only one platoon, the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon (26th ISDP), based first at Fort Riley, Kansas, survived intact. Before the war, this platoonâs main job was public demonstrations that showcased military dog capabilities to American audiences.

Scout dogs in Korea were not attack dogs in the way many people imagine war dogs to be. Their central task was to give a silent alert, typically by freezing, raising their hackles, or pointing, when they detected enemy soldiers ahead of a patrol, at an observation post, or forward of the front lines. Nearly all of these patrols took place at night, when human senses were least reliable, and the risk of walking into an ambush was highest.

Over the course of the war, the 26th ISDP conducted more than 1,500 combat patrols. A Review of after-action reports credited scout dog teams with reducing casualty rates among the patrols they accompanied by 65 percent, an extraordinary figure for a single battlefield innovation.

The dogs became well known, even feared, on the other side of the line, too. Historical accounts describe Chinese forces using loudspeakers along the front to broadcast messages to American troops that reportedly included the line, âYankee, take your dog and go home!â

Among the dogs of the 26th ISDP, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record: Scout Dog York, service number 011X. York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Other dogs in the platoon earned similar renown. Arlo, another German Shepherd, is remembered for helping his patrol avoid what is believed to have been a near-certain ambush. Handler accounts and unit histories also mention dogs named Happy, Champ, and Hasso as part of the platoonâs roster of effective scout teams during the conflict.

The 26th ISDP served in Korea from June 1951 until the July 1953 armistice. Over that time, its members, both human and canine alike, were awarded a total of three Silver Stars, six Bronze Stars for Valor, and thirty-five Bronze Stars for Meritorious Service. On February 27, 1953, the Department of the Army formally recognized the platoonâs accomplishments in General Order No. 21.

Unlike the individual medal controversies that followed Chips during WWII, official recognition of the Korean War scout dogs came largely through unit citations rather than personal decorations for the animals themselves, an approach that seems to have avoided the same public dispute over honoring dogs with human military awards.

Before the Korean War, the scout dog program had all but disappeared. In 1946, the Armyâs Committee on Organization at Fort Benning debated whether to keep infantry war dog platoons active. Committee chairman Brigadier General Frederick McCabe recommended retaining them and attaching them to infantry training units; a recommendation that was largely ignored. Instead, the Quartermaster Corps shifted toward purchasing dogs directly from breeders rather than sustaining a broader loan program with the public. Had the 26th ISDP not survived this postwar contraction, the United States might have entered Korea with no scout dog capability at all.

The success of the 26th ISDP in Korea, epitomized by dogs like York, helped ensure scout dogs would never again be allowed to disappear from the Armyâs order of battle as they had after 1945. When American forces deployed to Vietnam a little more than a decade later, the Army reactivated its scout dog program in 1965, drawing directly on lessons learned in Korea.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

He had just been shot through the face. He had lost an eye.

And still, Nemo crawled back to his wounded handler and lay across him, guarding him from anyone who came near.

This is the story of the Vietnam War's most famous sentry dog.

Spider plants can struggle in winter, and they'll soon let you know something's wrong with browning leaf tips.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spider plants are known for being among the easiest of all houseplants, all but foolproof – but no plant is truly indestructible. While a spider plant tends to thrive even in tough conditions, winter indoors is when these usually healthy houseplants can start to struggle. Shorter days, less light and colder temperatures trigger changes in growth. If you don’t change your care to match this shift, you could end up with dry, brown tips on your otherwise attractive and elegant spider plant leaves.

Brown tips on spider plant leaves is a common problem that dogs many houseplant parents through winter. It’s not a reason to panic, though. It rarely indicates a major underlying issue that could kill your plant, but you should treat it as a cry for help.

Spider plant care in winter is just as easy as summer care, once you know what your houseplant needs this season. Which of these crucial elements of winter care is your spider plant missing out on, that's leading to brown leaf tips?

Growth slows in winter, so your spider plant doesn’t need as much water as it did over the summer. Instead of watering on a regular schedule, go by feel. Stick your finger in the soil and if the top inch or two is dry, it’s time to water. Or take out the guesswork and use a cheap moisture meter like this from Amazon.

When you water your spider plant, give it a good soaking but let the water drain all the way through the soil and tip any excess out of the saucer. Don’t allow your plant to sit in a dish of water or for the soil to remain soggy due to poor drainage.

Spider plants are sensitive to some minerals common in most tap water, particularly fluoride. Minerals accumulate in the soil and can ultimately lead to browning leaves. Most home water filters don't remove fluoride so, if you think mineral accumulation might be the cause of those brown leaf tips, switch to distilled water like this from Walmart: a gallon costs a little over a dollar and it'll last for weeks.

You can also remove some of the build-up of minerals in the soil by flushing your houseplant once a month. Stand your spider plant in the sink and pour a generous amount of distilled water, or rainwater if you have it, through the pot, letting it all drain out through the bottom.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Reduced light levels is an environmental stress that can lead to unhealthy foliage. Your spider plant may have been perfectly happy in its window all summer and into the fall but now shortening days mean less light. Too little light might contribute to browning on foliage, but it also dulls the colors on leaves and reduces their natural variegation.

Try moving your plant to a location where the light is a little brighter, but still indirect. Rotate your plant regularly so it gets even light exposure. If natural light is limited in your home in winter, consider adding a grow light to supplement it, choosing a product with full-spectrum LEDs like this Glowrium Full Spectrum Smart Grow Light from Amazon.

Give your houseplants a boost through winter with this compact, full-spectrum grow light. Its adjustable gooseneck makes positioning easy, while the smart app lets you control brightness, set timers, and simulate sunrise and sunset.

Colder air is naturally dryer, but turning on winter heating can also sap moisture from the air. Most houseplants struggle with this drop in humidity from summer to winter and while it isn’t typically the primary issue that leads to brown leaves, it can stress plants and contribute to the problem.

The easiest way to increase humidity around houseplants is to DIY a humidifying tray or buy a readymade one like this Bonsai Humidity Tray from Lowe's, then set the pot on the pebbles and fill with water. Grouping plants together can help them create and hold onto a more humid microclimate, especially if one or more has a pebble tray. Misting leaves with water is only a temporary solution to an ongoing problem, so don’t waste your time on this task.

Along with changing light and humidity levels, temperature fluctuation as the heating turns on for the winter is another element of environmental stress that may contribute to damaged foliage on your spider plant. To keep temperatures around your houseplant more consistent, position it away from heating vents and radiators and out of cold drafts. If you want to see exactly what temperature swings your spider plant is putting up with, the results from an indoor thermometer like this from Amazon that records minimum and maximum levels might just surprise you!

As your spider plant slows its growth this winter, it needs fewer nutrients. If you continue fertilizing at the same rate you did during the growing season, excess nutrients will accumulate in the soil. This acts like a salt build-up, similar to what happens with tap water, that can burn leaf tips. The solution is to stop fertilizing until spring, and give the soil a good flush with distilled water or rainwater to eliminate some of the accumulated salts.

Winter spider plant care is all about not doing too much. Rather than giving yourself a list of care tasks, think about what you need to switch up for the slow season. Find the right spot for your plants for winter, use good water less often but provide plenty of humidity, and you'll encourage healthy, slow growth for next year. Get these aspects right and you can safely prune those unslightly brown leaf tips and rest assured that they won't return.

Nobody wants a Christmas tree shedding needles before the big day. Our expert reveals whether this unusual watering trick really makes a difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every December, someone ends up sweeping dry needles from under a Christmas tree that looked fresh just two weeks prior. A real tree that dries out too soon sheds needles onto the floor, fades in color, and becomes a greater fire risk as it loses moisture. Year after year, home tricks to keep one fresh get shared widely, and drilling holes in a Christmas tree trunk remains near the top of the list.

The usual advice on how to stop a Christmas tree drying out largely holds up fine. On paper, the drill trick makes sense too – more openings in the wood ought to let more water in, so why not add in a few holes below the waterline?

Folks who study cut Christmas tree care for a living have looked at that idea, though, and the drill doesn't come out of it looking good. Here's what Christmas tree drilling actually does, what to do if a tree quits drinking partway through the season, and how to make a real tree last longer.

No. Holes drilled into the trunk's base don't increase how much water a cut tree takes up. Devices that feed water through side holes don't keep a tree as fresh as a standard stand of plain water, either.

So how does a cut tree drink? Water moves up through the wood just under the bark, and those outer layers carry most of it. The trouble at the base is sap. After a trunk is cut, sap oozes out and dries over the end, slowly sealing it off. Holes in the bottom or side leave that seal in place, while a fresh horizontal cut across the base strips away the dried sap and exposes clean wood to the water.

Firstly, saw a clean, straight cut across the base. If the tree came off the stump more than about 12 hours ago, saw off a disk roughly ¼ to 1 inch (6 mm to 2.5 cm) thick and get it into water soon after. Trees cut at the farm that same morning can go directly into their stands.

Keep the cut flat across the trunk. Angled cuts and V-shaped points get suggested a lot, but they don't help the tree drink, and they make the trunk much harder to keep upright in the stand. Don't remove bark or shape the sides to fit into a smaller stand, because the outer wood absorbs water best. For a trunk that's too wide, get a larger stand – the Large or XL Krinner Tree Genie stand, available on Amazon, accommodates trunk diameters up to 7 inches (18 cm).

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One of the worst Christmas tree mistakes is letting water fall below the bottom of the trunk. Leave the cut end sitting in the air, and the sap seals it right back up, and then the tree can't take up water again until somebody saws off another slice. Plenty of stands still have water sitting in them after the trunk has lost contact, and from above everything looks fine. Bend down and look at where the water actually touches the trunk.

For forgetful households, you used to be able to buy a Snowflake water sensor, which hangs on the tree like an ornament and flashes when the water level runs low. The company has since gone out of business, but you can still pick up an unused one from eBay sellers for around $10. For a more hands-off solution, there's the HoHoHoH2o Automatic Christmas Tree Watering System, which monitors the water level in your stand and automatically tops it up when needed. It's cleverly disguised as a wrapped gift, so it blends right in under the tree.

A fresh tree drinks heavily early on and can go through more than a gallon (3.8 L) in a day, so check the stand at least daily for the first week and top it up as needed. Nobody enjoys crawling under low branches with a pitcher. This Kaiedos Christmas tree watering funnel tucks down into the stand on a long pole.

Freshness starts on the lot. Run your hand along a branch; very few needles should fall off, and the cut stump should feel sticky with sap. Good trees also feel heavy for their size and hold a rich green color.

If it has to wait a few days before coming inside, stand the trunk in a bucket of water in a cool, shaded spot like an unheated garage. At home, use a stand that holds about 1 quart (0.95 L) of water for every inch (2.5 cm) of trunk width, and at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) for most trees.

Cooler rooms slow down drying. Keep your tree well clear of fireplaces, heaters, heat vents, and sunny windows. LED lights give off far less heat than old incandescent strings, and it's a good habit to switch them off at bedtime. Skip the sugar, aspirin, bleach, soda, and other homemade preservatives. Store-bought products such as Miracle-Gro for Christmas Trees are also available, and thousands of reviewers claim they help keep trees hydrated and reduce needle drop. However, there's little independent evidence that additives work better than plain water.

If you suspect your Christmas tree is not drinking water, start by checking the stand. When the water level hasn't dropped in a day or two, see whether the trunk was ever above the waterline, and look for a dried crust of sap on the cut end. Trees that were very dry or very cold when they came home can also take a day or two to start drinking, so a slow start isn't always a sign of trouble.

If the base has sealed over and the tree isn't decorated yet, take it out and make another fresh cut. With a fully decorated tree, that's much harder, and drilling a few holes into the trunk below the waterline is sometimes offered as a fallback, though a fresh cut has far better support behind it. Once the needles feel brittle, break easily, or come off in your hand, the tree is too dry to save. Take it down, because a dried-out tree catches fire far more easily than a well-watered one.

So the drill can stay in the garage this year. A straight cut, a stand that never runs dry, and a cool spot away from heat do far more for your tree than any hole ever will, and they're less work, too. Keep the water topped up, and those needles should hang on through the holidays.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
